turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Dr. Smith, nice to meet you too. I came in today because... well, it's my husband’s sister. She’s been working this family business so she can get control of the money and push me out of all the decisions. And no matter how folks try to smooth it over, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now. 

People think you just don't notice things, you know? It’s just like when we went down to the county fair back in, oh, must have been 2019. They had this prize pumpkin, huge thing, and the man running the stall was trying to tell everyone he grew it without any chemicals, but you could see the empty fertilizer bags right there behind his truck! I told my husband right then, I said, people will just look you in the eye and lie to your face. We used to grow tomatoes in our backyard, big beefsteak ones. You gotta water them at the base, not the leaves, or they get that brown rot. My neighbor tried to tell me otherwise, but her garden was an absolute mess. I think she just bought her vegetables at the store and claimed she grew them. 

Anyway, what was I... oh, right, so I'm here because I'm just sick of everyone pretending I don't see exactly what his sister is up to.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, unwavering belief that her sister-in-law is plotting to control the family money and push her out, despite others' attempts to 'smooth it over'.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality and derailment, drifting from her chief complaint into a long, unrelated story about a county fair, pumpkins, and growing tomatoes before losing her train of thought and returning to the topic.

Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever hear voices or sounds that other people around you cannot hear?
turns.patient_response:
Voices? No, no, I don't hear anything like that. Just the usual things, you know. But speaking of hearing things, you wouldn't believe the noise my washing machine was making last week. It sounded like a bag of wrenches in a blender. I told my husband, I said, "That belt is going," but he wouldn't listen. He never listens. He just said it was off-balance. Off-balance! I've been doing laundry since I was twelve years old, I think I know what an off-balance load sounds like. 

It's just like that time we took his car to the mechanic over in Shelbyville. The man tried to tell us we needed a whole new transmission. I listened to the engine for two seconds and told him it was just a loose heat shield rattling around. Sure enough, ten dollar fix. But people will just try to pull one over on you if they think you aren't paying attention. Which is exactly what his sister is doing, thinking I don't hear the little side conversations she has with the accountant. But no, I don't hear any invisible voices or anything crazy like that.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing invisible voices or sounds that others cannot hear.

turns.doctor_question: Do you feel that most people you meet in your daily life are likely to be deceptive or have hidden agendas, or is this feeling specifically related to your husband's sister and the family business?
turns.patient_response:
Well, no, not everybody. Most folks are just trying to get by, you know? It's really just her and the way she runs that business. I mean, take Gary down at the hardware store. I was in there just Tuesday looking for some caulk for the guest bathroom. You know how the grout gets all crumbly around the edges of the tub if you don't seal it right? My husband tried to use that cheap clear silicone stuff last year and it peeled right off, just like string cheese. I told him he needed the sanded kind, but he just grabbed whatever was on the clearance endcap. 

Anyway, Gary spent twenty minutes helping me find the exact right tube. He’s a good egg, Gary is. His oldest daughter just had a baby, actually... a little girl, seven pounds something. Cute as a button, he showed me a picture on his phone. They named her Hazel, which I think is making a comeback, those older names. 

So no, I don't go around thinking everyone at the grocery store or the bank has some big secret agenda against me. People like Gary are perfectly fine. It's just my husband's sister. I know exactly what she's doing with those accounts, and she's definitely trying to pull the rug out from under me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient maintains a fixed, persecutory belief that her sister-in-law is secretly manipulating accounts to ruin her.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, wandering off-topic to discuss hardware store caulk, her husband's DIY mistakes, and a store clerk's new granddaughter before returning to the original question.

turns.doctor_question: Are there any other situations or beliefs you have, perhaps regarding your health or your body, that you feel are definitely true even though others might disagree with you?
turns.patient_response:
My health? No, I mean, I feel fine. I don't have any strange ideas about my body or anything. I mean, my knees ache a bit when it rains, but who doesn't have that at my age? Actually, speaking of rain, did you see that storm we had last weekend? The wind was just howling. It blew our heavy trash can all the way down the driveway and right into Mrs. Higgins' prize rose bushes. She was out there the next morning in her pink bathrobe, just glaring at our house. I mean, I felt bad, but it’s not like I control the weather! 

She’s always been a bit particular about her yard, though. Last summer, she hired this landscaping company, these young guys who played their radio so loud you couldn't hear yourself think. They planted all these petunias, but they put them right where the sun bakes the soil by two o'clock. I could have told her they'd fry, and sure enough, two weeks later, they looked like dried tea leaves. 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, my health. Yeah, no, I'm perfectly healthy. Nothing wrong with me at all, just dealing with all the stress from my husband's sister.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality, wandering off-topic to discuss the weather, a neighbor's yard, and landscaping before eventually returning to the doctor's question.

turns.doctor_question: Do you believe that your sister-in-law is working alone in this, or is she part of a larger group or organization that is trying to harm you?
turns.patient_response:
Well, working alone... I mean, she's definitely the one pulling the strings. It's just her and that accountant of hers, whispering whenever I walk into the room. But a larger group? No, no, I don't think she's part of the mafia or the government or anything silly like that. She's not smart enough for that anyway. 

Speaking of not being smart, you should have seen the way she tried to make a turkey last Thanksgiving. I swear, she didn't even thaw the bird all the way through. She just shoved it in the oven, frozen solid in the middle. We sat down to eat at four o'clock, and when my husband went to carve it, blood just ran right out onto the platter. It was a disaster. We ended up ordering Chinese food. The Golden Dragon down on 4th Street, they were the only place open. Have you ever had their crab rangoon? Oh, it is just to die for. They put a little bit of scallion in the cream cheese, which really makes a difference. I tried to make it at home once, but getting those little wonton wrappers folded right is harder than it looks. They kept popping open in the hot oil, and then you just have a mess of cream cheese floating around in your FryDaddy. 

But no, to answer your question, it's just her. Just her being sneaky and trying to ruin everything.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, persecutory belief that her sister-in-law is 'pulling the strings' and 'trying to ruin everything.'
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality by drifting from the topic of her sister-in-law into a lengthy, unrelated story about a Thanksgiving turkey, Chinese food, and frying crab rangoon.

turns.doctor_question: Has this situation with your sister-in-law caused you to stop doing things you normally enjoy, or has it affected your ability to keep up with your daily responsibilities at home?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, no, not at all. I still do all my regular things. I keep up with my quilting group, for one. Actually, we're working on a starburst pattern right now for the church raffle, and Brenda—she’s the one who organizes the blocks—she brought in this neon green fabric last week. I just don't know what she was thinking. I mean, it completely clashes with the autumn colors we all agreed on back in September. But you know Brenda, she always has to do her own thing. She’s the exact same way at potlucks, always brings some weird kale salad that nobody wants to eat when everyone else just wants a nice potato casserole. 

But anyway, yeah, I still do that, and my choir practice, and my GED lessons... I'm really pushing to get that diploma finally. Oh, and my senior walks! We do the mall walking on Tuesday mornings. Let me tell you, walking past that Cinnabon before you've had breakfast is just pure torture. That cinnamon sugar smell just hangs in the air right outside the Macy's entrance. 

So my daily life is fine. The house is clean, dinner's on the table. Really, the only thing that's changed is just... well, how much I trust my husband's sister. I just don't. And it definitely affects which family gatherings I feel comfortable going to nowadays. If I know she's going to be there, trying to act all innocent and sweet, I just make an excuse and stay home.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient denies failing to keep up with daily responsibilities, stating that her house is clean and dinner is on the table.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient explicitly denies losing interest in activities she normally enjoys, confirming she still actively participates in her quilting group, choir practice, and senior walks.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you felt that your sister-in-law has been trying to manipulate the family business?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it’s been going on for about a year and two months now. It all really started right around the time we had those big arguments with my husband's sister over the family care planning. We were trying to figure out the arrangements, you know, and we had to go visit all these different assisted living places. 

We toured this one over in Westlake... oh, what was it called? Shady Pines? No, Maple Ridge. Anyway, they had this gorgeous koi pond right in the main lobby. Just huge orange and white fish swimming around in there. I used to have a goldfish when I was a little girl. I won him at the county fair tossing ping pong balls into those little glass bowls. You know the game I'm talking about? I named him Barnaby. He lived for a surprisingly long time, almost four years! Well, until my brother accidentally knocked the bowl over while he was practicing his golf swing in the living room. My mother was just furious. Not even just about poor Barnaby, but because the dirty fish water stained the good rug. She tried club soda, she tried baking soda, but that water mark never fully came out. She ended up having to put a heavy oak armchair right over that spot just to hide it for the next ten years.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient confirms the persistent belief that her sister-in-law is manipulating the family business, stating it has been going on for a year and two months.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from the original topic of her sister-in-law to assisted living facilities, a koi pond, a childhood goldfish, and a stained rug without ever returning to the point.
